name: Testosterone pellets (Testopel)

card.summary: Rice-grain testosterone implants placed under the skin for months-long TRT; an established medical option with observational and small-trial data.
card.note: Requires a minor in-office procedure; compounded pellets are not FDA-approved products.

quick.overview:
Testosterone pellets are small solid implants placed under the skin that release testosterone gradually. Testopel is the FDA-approved brand; the US approved implantable pellets in 1972 for testosterone deficiency, and they returned to wider clinical use in recent years.

They appeal to people who want to avoid frequent injections or daily gels. Published work consists mainly of observational studies and a few small trials, not long-term outcome trials.
quick.mechanism: Pellets are inserted subcutaneously, typically in the hip or buttock area, and slowly dissolve, releasing testosterone into the bloodstream over several months. Medication overviews list dosing every 3 to 6 months, with pellets in 50, 75, 100 and 200 mg strengths.
quick.risks: Because the pellets are implanted, a minor procedure is needed, and reported complications of implant procedures include infection and pellet extrusion. As with other testosterone therapy, effects include acne, raised red blood cell counts, sperm suppression and other systemic effects. Compounded pellets are not the same as the branded FDA-approved product.

lead: Testosterone pellets are small cylindrical implants of crystalline testosterone placed under the skin to provide sustained hormone release. Testopel is the branded product; a 2012 multi-institution study notes that the FDA approved implantable testosterone pellets in 1972 for testosterone deficiency syndrome, and that clinical use was limited until Testopel was reintroduced [1].

Medication references list pellet doses of 150 to 1,200 mg every 3 to 6 months for men, in strengths of 50 to 200 mg per pellet [4]. Pellets are one of several delivery options alongside injections, gels and oral products [4].

Evidence consists of observational serum-level studies, patient-preference surveys and small randomised trials, mostly in men with diagnosed hypogonadism [1][2][3]. No published trials have examined pellets for appearance outcomes in healthy people.

paras: Pellets are used for testosterone replacement in men with deficiency [1]. A single-centre trial also compared compounded and branded pellets in men with testosterone deficiency [3]. A registered phase 1 trial tested pellets together with vitamins D and E in Peyronie's disease [6].

A multi-institution observational study combined databases from six academic centres to characterise serum testosterone levels after Testopel insertion [1]. A randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial compared a compounded pellet (E100) with Testopel in men with testosterone deficiency to assess both safety and efficacy [3]. A further phase 3 registration compares Testopel with generic pellets in 75 men [5].
A survey-based study of 175 men at an academic urology practice examined what led patients to start or stop pellets compared with gels and injections [2].

General testosterone therapy effects include acne, oily skin and hair loss, sperm suppression, and warnings related to cardiovascular events, prostate conditions and blood pressure; testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy [4]. Implantation is a minor surgical procedure, which makes procedure-related events such as infection a topic in the pellet literature.

Pellets are offered through urology and hormone clinics and are also prepared by compounding pharmacies, which the 2023 trial compared against the branded product [3]. Testosterone is a controlled substance in the US [4].

Observational data show serum testosterone levels after Testopel insertion across six academic centres [1]. A 2023 randomised trial compared compounded and branded pellets [3], and a phase 3 trial (NCT04523480, 75 men, completed) compared Testopel with generic pellets [5]. A phase 1 trial (NCT01578473, 75 participants) tested pellets for Peyronie's disease [6]. No studies found for appearance or physique outcomes in healthy people.

timeline.event: FDA approves implantable testosterone pellets for testosterone deficiency [1].
Six-institution observational study of Testopel serum levels published [1].
Randomised trial compares compounded and branded pellets [3].
